title: This Graph of Data Center Spending Compared to All Other Construction Will Give You Chills
source_used: Futurism (full text from the main session's fulltext copy); it reports on an essay by Derek Thompson, which was not read
key_facts: Futurism reports on a new essay by the podcaster and writer Derek Thompson about key economic measures around AI in 2026.
Thompson uses data from Harvard Kennedy School economist Jason Furman in a bar graph of construction spending growth.
Data centre construction grew 64.5% in the most recent year; new energy infrastructure grew 4.1%.
Multi-family home building fell 5.6%; healthcare and commercial retail construction each fell 10.1%; educational construction fell 12.6%; manufacturing shrank nearly 24% from 2025 to 2026.
Futurism's own framing: US growth is 'anything but healthy' and 'predicated almost entirely on the AI boom'; with investors growing sceptical, data centre spending could fall back.
Futurism describes Thompson as known for his 'abundance' policy agenda; the date and place of his essay are not given.
quote_evidence: By the numbers, data center construction has grown at a rate of 64.5 percent in the most recent year, while new energy infrastructure has grown by 4.1 percent to keep pace — since demand is growing for electricity to power the AI boom.
Using data from Harvard Kennedy School economist Jason Furman, Thompson shows that growth in data center construction has exploded this year, while all but one other category has regressed.
Yet as new economic data shows, that growth is anything but healthy, and predicated almost entirely on the AI boom.
why_it_matters_hint: US building outside data centres is shrinking, so the economy leans heavily on AI construction, according to one writer's reading of Furman's data.
event_date: Futurism published 11 Oct 2026 14:01 UTC; the essay's date is not stated
notes: Relay of a relay: Futurism summarises Thompson's essay, which uses Furman's data; neither the essay nor the data were read. Futurism's judgments (unhealthy growth, a possible fall) are the outlet's opinion, kept separate in the entry.
